glossary: Attack surface
Everything about a domain that is reachable or visible from the internet: hostnames, IP addresses, open ports, services, software banners and third-party providers.
A / AAAA
DNS records mapping a name to an IPv4 (A) or IPv6 (AAAA) address.
CNAME
An alias from one name to another; the apex of a domain cannot normally be a CNAME.
MX
Mail exchanger records naming the servers that receive mail for the domain.
NS
Nameserver records naming the authoritative DNS servers for the domain.
SOA
Start of Authority: the primary nameserver, the responsible mailbox and the zone's timing values.
TXT
Free-form text records used for SPF, domain verification tokens and other policies.
CAA
Records naming the certificate authorities allowed to issue certificates for the domain.
HSTS
HTTP Strict Transport Security: a response header telling browsers to use only HTTPS for the site for a set period.
Banner
Software name or version disclosed in a response header, such as Server: Apache/2.4.58.

narrative: H1 mapped what test.c4lab.in exposes to the internet. It resolves to 107.180.237.42, DNS is hosted by your DNS hosting provider, email is handled by DreamHost Mail and the domain is registered with GoDaddy.
The HTTPS site returns HTTP 200 from Apache; TCP 80 is open; TCP 443 is open.
The most significant issue is H1-001 “X-Powered-By header discloses application technology” (low). X-Powered-By: PHP/5.6.40

Other findings: H1-002 “HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) not enforced” (low); H1-003 “Server header discloses web server software” (informational); H1-004 “Public DNS reveals third-party services” (informational).
Controls in good shape: http://test.c4lab.in returns 301 redirecting to https://test.c4lab.in/.

findings.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) not enforced
findings.about: Checks for a Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header with a max-age of at least six months, which tells browsers to use only HTTPS for the site.
findings.analysis: No Strict-Transport-Security header on the HTTPS response.
findings.what_we_found: The HTTPS response from https://test.c4lab.in has no Strict-Transport-Security header.
why_it_matters: Even with an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, a browser's first request to http://test.c4lab.in goes out unencrypted, and the redirect itself can be intercepted. HSTS tells the browser to rewrite every future http:// request to https:// itself, before anything is sent, and to refuse to click through certificate warnings for the site.
findings.attack_scenario: SSL stripping (sslstrip): an attacker on the network intercepts the initial HTTP request, suppresses the redirect and proxies the site to the victim over HTTP while talking HTTPS to the real server.
findings.severity_rationale: Low: requires an on-path attacker and a user who reaches the site over HTTP first.

fix_steps.text: Apache (.htaccess or virtual host, with mod_headers):

fix_steps: Start with a short max-age (for example 300) and increase it once every subdomain works over HTTPS. includeSubDomains applies the policy to every subdomain.
Optionally, once stable, add "; preload" and submit the domain at hstspreload.org so browsers enforce HTTPS from the first visit.
findings.rollback: Set max-age=0 to tell browsers to forget the policy.

findings.title: Server header discloses web server software
findings.about: Checks whether the Server response header discloses the web server product or version.
findings.analysis: Server: Apache discloses the product but not its version.
findings.what_we_found:
https://test.c4lab.in returns the header:
Server: Apache
The product is disclosed but not its version.
why_it_matters: Knowing the product (Apache) narrows down which attacks and misconfigurations to try. It is minor because the version is hidden and the product can usually be identified by other means anyway.
findings.attack_scenario: Product-specific probing, such as Apache-specific paths and modules, without needing to fingerprint first.
findings.severity_rationale: Informational: product-only banners are common and give little advantage.
fix_steps: No action is required. If you control the server and want to remove the header entirely, use a reverse proxy or CDN that rewrites it, or Apache's mod_security SecServerSignature.
findings.remediation: No action is required. If you control the server and want to remove the header entirely, use a reverse proxy or CDN that rewrites it, or Apache's mod_security SecServerSignature.

findings.title: Public DNS reveals third-party services
findings.about: Identifies the third-party services the domain's public DNS reveals (email, DNS and web hosts, SaaS verification tokens and SPF senders), the information an attacker gathers first.
findings.analysis: 1 third-party services identified from public DNS.
findings.what_we_found:
Public DNS for test.c4lab.in reveals these providers and services:
• Email: DreamHost Mail (MX mx1.dreamhost.com)
why_it_matters: This is normal and largely unavoidable: SPF, MX and verification records must be public to work. It is reported so you know exactly what an attacker learns in seconds.

Each service is a phishing pretext ("Your Google Workspace password expires today") and an account to protect. Verification tokens for services you no longer use add noise and can indicate forgotten accounts still linked to the domain.
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker sees that test.c4lab.in uses DreamHost Mail for email and clones that provider's login page for a targeted credential-phishing campaign against your staff.
findings.severity_rationale: Informational: no misconfiguration. Exposure is inherent to how these records work.
fix_steps: Remove verification TXT records and SPF includes for services you no longer use. In your DNS hosting provider: Open the control panel of the provider that hosts the domain's DNS (the nameservers listed in this report) and add or edit the record there.
Enforce multi-factor authentication on every listed service, especially the email provider (DreamHost Mail) and the DNS host (your DNS hosting provider), whose accounts control the domain.
Brief staff that phishing will imitate these specific providers.

verify.expected: Only records for services in active use.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1590.002 — Gather Victim Network Information: DNS
MITRE ATT&CK T1593 — Search Open Websites/Domains

findings.remediation: Remove verification TXT records and SPF includes for services you no longer use. In your DNS hosting provider: Open the control panel of the provider that hosts the domain's DNS (the nameservers listed in this report) and add or edit the record there.

technical_sections.title: DNS footprint
technical_sections.subtitle: What public DNS reveals about the domain
technical_sections.intro: Each record type is listed with what it tells an attacker. Values are exactly as returned by dig.

items.label: A (IPv4)
items.explanation: IPv4 addresses the domain's website resolves to. An attacker uses these to find the hosting provider and to look for other sites and services on the same IP addresses.

items.label: AAAA (IPv6)
items.explanation: IPv6 addresses. Services reachable over IPv6 sometimes have weaker firewall rules than their IPv4 equivalents.

items.label: CNAME
items.explanation: An apex alias, if any. CNAMEs pointing at deprovisioned third-party services are the classic source of subdomain takeovers.

items.label: MX
items.explanation: Mail servers. They reveal the email provider, which tells an attacker which login page to clone for credential phishing.

items.label: NS
items.explanation: Authoritative nameservers. They reveal the DNS host; whoever controls that account controls the domain's website and email.

items.label: SOA
items.explanation: The primary nameserver, the responsible-party mailbox and the zone's refresh, retry, expire and minimum TTL timers.

items.label: TXT
items.explanation: TXT records: SPF, verification tokens and other policies. They reveal the SaaS services the organisation uses.

items.label: CAA
items.explanation: Certificate authorities allowed to issue certificates. An empty list means any CA may issue.

items.label: Delegation trace
items.value: completed from the root to the domain's nameservers
items.explanation: Whether a full trace from the root servers reached the domain's nameservers.

items.label: host cross-check
value: test.c4lab.in mail is handled by 10 mx1.dreamhost.com.
items.explanation: A second resolver client confirming the address and mail records.

items.label: Registrar
items.explanation: The company the domain is registered through. Its account controls the domain's nameservers.

items.label: Created
items.explanation: Registration date.

items.label: Expires
items.explanation: If this date passes without renewal, the domain can be lost.

items.label: Last updated
items.explanation: Last change to the registration record.

items.label: EPP status
items.explanation: Registry locks. clientTransferProhibited blocks unauthorised transfers.
